💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission.
  • In a recent development, I had just finished pitching my tent and inflating my sleeping pad on a recent trip, and I could not wait to tear open the packet of dried miso soup I’d packed.
  • Sources indicate that canister stoves, like the ones most backpackers use during the summer hiking season, perform poorly when the mercury drops.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

In a recent development, I had just finished pitching my tent and inflating my sleeping pad on a recent trip, and I could not wait to tear open the packet of dried miso soup I’d packed. My fingers were chilled from fiddling with guylines, and I craved the feeling of a steaming cup cradled in my hands. I screwed my ultralight stove onto a fuel canister, squeezed some water from my filter bag into a pot, and lit up. And then I proceeded to wait for what felt like ages. The flame was low and weak. Had I packed a nearly empty canister? No. The feeble flame was a harbinger, much like the leaves littering the trail: Winter was coming.

Sources indicate that canister stoves, like the ones most backpackers use during the summer hiking season, perform poorly when the mercury drops. Cold temperatures lower the internal pressure of the canister, causing it to falter, sputter, or produce a smaller flame. Regular winter campers often solve this problem by packing liquid fuel stoves like the MSR Whisperlite, which perform well in below freezing temperatures. Some canister stoves have a built-in pressure regulator that helps them stay efficient in the cold. But not every backpacker wants to shell out for an entire quiver of camp stoves. That’s where a little innovation comes in: Keeping a canister warm, even when the ambient temperature is frigid, helps maintain pressure so you can boil water on a regular canister stove all year round. Do it the wrong way, however and you might end up scorching more than your food.

When it comes to boosting the efficiency of your canister stove in winter, the key is gentle warming. A fuel canister’s contents are pressurized; when it is cold out, your goal is to increase that pressure ever so slightly. But overheating—and thus overpressurizing—can cause the canister to explode.

Warnings printed on the side of a canister tell this tale. Most manufacturers caution users to keep a canister below 120°F. Heating a canister by rapid means, like placing it in boiling water is a very bad idea—just ask the guy who punched a hole in his ceiling trying to heat a canister for a fuel transfer.

Recent findings suggest that how else can one warm a canister? One hiker on Reddit suggested sticking a chemical hand warmer next to the canister and enclosing it in an insulated pouch. But experts Backpacker spoke to did not recommend that method.

“You’re adding a continuous heat source while also insulating the canister, and there’s no particularly good way to monitor or control its temperature,” states Adam Wilcox, senior mechanical design engineer at Jetboil.

Recent findings suggest that hothands, manufacturer of popular chemical warmers, claims that their products reach an average of 135°F, and warns that the maximum temperature can surpass 158°F. Granted, this doesn’t mean that placing a hand warmer beside your fuel canister will immediately warm the fuel contents to that same temperature, but it does heighten your risk of dangerously increasing  the pressure. Gentle warming is a safer bet.

According to recent reports, “Body heat before use or a controlled warm-water bath are much more predictable ways of warming a cold canister,” states Wilcox. “The key with water is warm, not hot, and avoiding excessive heating of the canister.”.

For a quick boil, keeping the fuel canister inside your jacket for a few minutes prior to use may do the trick to increase internal pressure. Of course, the effects of this will diminish rather quickly as you run your stove and expose the canister to cold air. If you need to run your stove a little longer to cook a meal or melt snow, a warm water bath can provide safe, continuous warming. Place your fuel canister inside a dish or spare pot. (I like to carry a collapsible silicone bowl for this purpose.) Light your stove. As soon as the water begins to warm but before it boils, pour some into the dish surrounding your canister. You should immediately notice improved performance.

Sources indicate that shopping for a upcoming stove? Springing for one with a pressure regulator can help it perform more consistently across seasons. MSR claims that its Pocket Rocket Deluxe can run at full power at a fuel canister pressure of as little as 16.5 PSI. (A full canister would typically be at 45 PSI at room temperature.).

#33301. The Glacier Died—And the Trail Runners Started Coming

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2686 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Trailrunnermag ↗ Open Full Page

The Glacier Died—And the Trail Runners Started Coming

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2686 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’m standing with Samuel Mendoza on top of Chacaltaya Mountain, 17,785 feet above sea level.
  • Directly ahead, the Altiplano—the high plain—stretches from the foot of the mountain.
  • Behind us rises the Huayna Potosí massif.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’m standing with Samuel Mendoza on top of Chacaltaya Mountain, 17,785 feet above sea level. Under our feet is a sharp slope of scree, a jumbled descent of rocks with patches of snow. The air is thin, and the vast Bolivian landscape surrounds us.

Directly ahead, the Altiplano—the high plain—stretches from the foot of the mountain. El Alto, the chaotic concrete and red brick city that has grown to roughly 900,000 people, lies at the far edge of the plain at 13,000 feet of elevation, crammed against a canyon’s edge. About 1,500 feet below and connected by a series of cable cars, La Paz, Bolivia’s seat of government, sprawls.

Behind us rises the Huayna Potosí massif. The nearly 20,000-foot summit towers above, its glaciated peak passing in and out of fast-moving clouds. About 45 miles to the northwest, Lake Titicaca—the central motif to Inca creation stories—shimmers on the horizon.

It’s here, on this high mountain of almost-bare rock cradled in the Andes, that Mendoza learned to ski.

According to recent reports, located roughly 20 miles north of La Paz, Chacaltaya was once the world’s highest-altitude ski resort. It began in the 1930s when Raúl Posnansky, an engineer and ski enthusiast, recognized the mountain’s potential, according to 2023 reporting by “Radio Ambulante.” Chacaltaya’s glacier, though relatively small in area at roughly 55 acres, was a solid tongue of ice descending the slope. Temperatures up high stayed low, and snow fell heavily and often during the wet season. The ice was there, had always been there, and would always be there, by all indications at the time.

Posnansky worked to materialize his skiing fantasy: He hired laborers to build an access road, haul materials, construct cabins, and install the first rope tow at Chacaltaya—powered by a truck engine housed in a cabin hanging over the base of the ski run.

It has been revealed that posnansky, along with other mountain athletes, founded the Club Andino Boliviano, a group of dedicated skiers and enthusiasts. To fund the growing ski scene, the club drew involvement from La Paz’s middle and upper classes, and Posnansky and the club persuaded Bolivia’s Congress to pass tax legislation dedicating 1% of the country’s hotel revenue to Bolivia’s Ski and Mountaineering Federation. This funding would help transform Chacaltaya from a passion project into the hub of Bolivian skiing—a hub that, while retaining its roughshod, backyard roots, would grow to host a national ski team, crowded weekend races, the first South American ski championships, and athletes who would represent the country at Winter Olympics.

Recent findings suggest that when Mendoza was a young boy in El Alto, his family wasn’t connected to La Paz’s urban elite who would drive across the Altiplano to ski. Mendoza’s father, however, worked as the caretaker of Chacaltaya, often living for weeks at a time at the resort to maintain the facilities.

When he was 15, Mendoza accompanied his father to the mountain for the first time. He spent his first night at the base racked by altitude sickness.

“My dad gave me coca leaf tea,” he says. The next day, “the sun came out; I felt better. I got acclimated, and I learned to ski.”.

Fifty years later, standing once again on the summit, Mendoza is transported back to the resort’s heyday.

“The rope would drop us off here,” he claims. “And then …” He puts his hands on bent knees and waves them back and forth in a slalom. He raises his hands over his head and lets out a high yell, feeling the old rush of racing in the cold air.

Sources indicate that mendoza is in his 60s now. He has a harder time seeing, looking out through thick glasses, and his knees sometimes bother him.

Around us the glacier has completely vanished, leaving behind only a mountain of rock.

Industry observers note that infatuated with the world of snow and slopes, Mendoza learned to ski on gear borrowed from Club Andino. He worked long, physical days with his father, tasks ranging from construction and upkeep to manning the rope tow—including rebraiding the wire cable whenever it snapped, a job that left Mendoza with thin white scars across his fingers. From his father, he learned to manage the mountain, the two often sleeping in the lodge for weeks at a time.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, his love for skiing only deepened. Mendoza remembers Stanley Shepard, an American diplomat posted in Bolivia, who taught him advanced techniques and shared the joy of the mountain.

“Stan would drive up this road so fast,” he indicates as we drive the same route from the city to Chacaltaya some 50 years later. He smiles with the memory of the adrenaline rush.

In a recent development, mendoza’s ski story exists in a split reality: In one, he is the caretaker’s son, surrounded by a country’s elites who lived near, but not next to, families like his. The socioeconomic divide paralleled the geography: La Paz’s wealthy neighborhoods in the valley, El Alto on the cold outcropping of the Altiplano above. Despite the divide, Mendoza was a vital member of the Chacaltaya scene; the members of Club Andino were his friends. The nights were full of music whenever others would sleep alongside him and his father at the refugio. The period is marked in Mendoza’s mind by shared meals in the cabin and shared runs on the mountain.

By the 1970s, with Chacaltaya entering its golden period, Mendoza was both employee and skier. He tells me he used to set up for the weekend slalom races—ones he’d often compete in as well. I ask about the slalom poles, curious about infrastructure. He tells me they were made nearby. “But the first times,” he states, “we used hollow canes, like cornstalks.”.

In a 1976 article in Ski Magazine, American writer Jeff Frees described his visit to the ski hill. There were some two dozen weekly skiers sharing the piste and “a slightly doglegged swath of snow” that was “lined with rocks from top to bottom,” although there were no lift lines, he writes.

The chalet, perched on a rocky precipice, was “so frightening and insecure-looking,” that “some skiers refused to enter it,” Frees says. With the altitude nearing 18,000 feet, other visitors didn’t even bother trying, exiting the minibus up from La Paz only to climb into the truck heading back down the road.

In a recent development, this was the electric, eclectic golden period. One 1,000-foot run served by a single rope tow prone to snapping and powered by a truck engine. A handful of foreign visitors and the dedicated group of Club Andino members. A small, warm refugio built on a cliffside, filled with coca tea, quinoa soup, and music. Weekend races and training events for young locals, supporting ski teams who would go on to participate in four consecutive Olympics starting in 1980. And behind this incredible scene was Samuel Mendoza.

According to recent reports, “It was frozen all the time,” Mendoza says. “The people said, ‘This is forever. It will never recede.’”.

“But little by little, it started to thaw.”.

According to recent reports, scientists had been documenting Chacaltaya for decades, but a systematic study of the glacier began in 1991, led in part by Edson Ramírez of the Universidad Mayor de San Andrés in La Paz (UMSA). Glaciologists’ observations began to echo the concerns skiers had voiced for years: Chacaltaya was melting—and fast.

“Snow would fall at night,” Mendoza says, “but it would be gone by midday.” As temperatures rose, the glacier retreated, exposing more and more of the rock underneath.

While the retreat was evident in some of the earliest photos from the 1940s, Ramírez and his team found that, in just six years from 1992 to 1998, the glacier’s melt had accelerated dramatically, losing more than 40% of its surface area and roughly two-thirds of its ice volume. The team’s prediction: The glacier would disappear within 10 to 15 years.

By 2009, the glacier was completely gone.

“The entire glacier of the world’s highest ski slope had turned to water,” Mendoza reflects.

Recent findings suggest that as the ski run melted under them, various last-ditch efforts were implemented to keep the sport alive. Artificial snow production was attempted, but ultimately proved too costly. Moving the resort to other nearby mountains was considered, but transportation and access were constant hurdles. Even traditional Andean rituals were offered to the mountain gods.

But the glacier, once gone, would not come back.

According to recent reports, without their ski hub, the Club Andino eventually unraveled. A photo hangs in the abandoned refugio of smiling members piled outside the club. Mendoza tells me their names—a running list of friends moved abroad or passed away. Even their headquarters in La Paz is now shuttered.

While sooner than expected, Chacaltaya’s glacier death was not unique within the broader scope of Andean glaciers. Research published in 2026 by Giuliana Adrianzen and Andrew Malone of the University of Illinois Chicago found that Bolivia’s Cordillera Real lost a stunning 42% of its glaciated area between 1992 and 2024.

This trend is widespread across the Andes, which are home to 99% of the world’s tropical glacier area—particularly vulnerable ice fields located near the Earth’s equator.

In a recent development, glaciers in this latitudinal band are much more susceptible to small temperature changes than those outside of it. Kept frozen primarily by extreme altitude, tropical glaciers already exist close to the temperature threshold to sustain permanent ice; they also don’t experience the long, cold winters of glaciers nearer the poles. Andean glaciers are now thinning 35% faster than the global average, according to a 2025 international report co-authored by researchers at the University of Sheffield. As global warming pushes the freezing level higher, more precipitation falls on these glaciers as rain instead of snow, accelerating the melt.

Sources indicate that over the 60 years between 1960 and 2020, Peru lost 56% of its glacier area. In 2024, Venezuela was declared glacier-free with the death of the Humboldt Glacier (named, perhaps ominously, after the German naturalist who pioneered the notion that everything in the natural world is connected). Colombia is following the same trajectory, having lost more than 90% of its glaciated area since the mid-1800s.

According to UNESCO, the Andes could lose 78 to 97% of their tropical glacier volume by the year 2100.

Of course, more than skiing is at risk—including the water supply risk of some 90 million people across the Andes. These glaciers serve as water reserves for the millions of people who live downstream, and their disappearance foreshadows looming ecological disasters. Many Andean municipalities also rely on hydroelectric power, which depends on steady dry-season meltwater from the glaciers. As the glaciers shrink, that flow is dwindling, increasing the severity of droughts.

While Chacaltaya’s lift has long since stopped spinning, a handful of trained guides and foreign clients continue to practice ski mountaineering in Bolivia, climbing high peaks and bombing descents on still-intact glaciers. While the chalet has ceased to function, the mountain remains an active scientific base. The Chacaltaya Observatory, run by UMSA’s Laboratory for Atmospheric Physics—with multiple international collaborators—continues to measure the atmosphere, climate, and cosmic rays.

And although skiing has abandoned the mountain, Mendoza has not.

Recent findings suggest that since his father died on Chacaltaya over 30 years ago, Mendoza has served as the mountain’s main caretaker, a position he continues to hold. He spends more time in El Alto with his family now, but he and his brother Adolfo still make multiple trips a week to Chacaltaya, welcoming the handful of tourists who come to visit the abandoned chalet or use it as an acclimatization hike. With the small collected entrance fees, he pays for repairs and maintains his memories of the resort.

Many of Mendoza’s days, however, are spent in solitude, standing alone at 17,000 feet on Chacaltaya’s rocky remains.

“When you’re alone it’s a little sad,” he says. “With only the birds, the condors, the Andean foxes.”.

Sources indicate that since the collapse of the glacier, a new group of athletes has taken to Chacaltaya: trail runners—whose arrival is directly tied to skiing’s disappearance. Paolo Choque is the director of skyrunning for the Bolivian Ski and Mountaineering Federation. One of the “last people to learn to ski in Bolivia,” Choque witnessed the collapse of skiing at Chacaltaya, and he has since helped cultivate trail running to take its place.

Sources indicate that in 2001, when Choque learned to ski, the main chunk of the glacier was already “ruined,” he notes. Against the backdrop of the dying mountain, Choque became involved in promoting skiing and snowboarding in Bolivia, including searching for alternative mountains to host competitions.

In 2011, the federation found another suitable slope at nearby Charquini and hosted a Bolivian Ski Championship. Choque notes that snowboarding grew in popularity over a handful of years with the promotion efforts, but participation numbers remained low—with just 25 racers in the snowboard event in 2015. Amid melting ice and low participation, he made the decision to pivot. “I said, ‘No, this isn’t going anywhere. We don’t even have a ski slope.’”.

Inspired by the sport’s explosion in Spain, Choque organized a pilot skyrunning race on Chacaltaya in 2016, which was met with a strong reception. Athletes had returned to the mountain. The federation’s championship now draws about 200 participants each year, according to Choque. Racers gain points at multiple events across the country, which take place over otherworldly terrain—from the world’s largest salt flats in Uyuni to the folds of the Sajama stratovolcano, the shores of Lake Titicaca, and, of course, Chacaltaya Mountain.

“Skiing may have died,” Choque states, “but mountain sports have not.”.

According to recent reports, while private trail races have also increased in popularity in Bolivia over the past decade, the federation aims to develop skyrunning and its next generation of athletes through accessible competition. Race entries, Choque emphasizes, are kept inexpensive, and youth competition categories give athletes the opportunity to qualify for international competition.

“For me, sport must come first, and it must be accessible to everyone,” Choque says.

Despite challenges with funding, Choque states the federation has seen success in sending participants to compete in the South American Championships, where they have earned podium finishes, including three medals in 2025.

As one sport fades and another grows, Choque defines what success could look like for Bolivian skyrunning.

“What I want to achieve is to bring a South American championship here, and if possible, even a youth world championship to Bolivia,” he indicates. “We have the potential.”.

Paolo and the federation hope that Chacaltaya will continue to be an crucial mountain hub for decades to come—with or without the glacier.

For all of the uniqueness of Chacaltaya’s history, it does mirror a larger global skiing trend: most of the participants were wealthy. Mendoza remembers well the divide caused by the cost of equipment. “From the city of El Alto there weren’t a lot of skiers,” he states.

Recent findings suggest that through the Ski and Mountaineering Federation, Choque is determined that the next iteration of Chacaltaya’s mountain sports—trail and sky running—do not follow the same pattern. Mendoza, meanwhile, has seen some of the runners who are taking to the mountain to train where he once skied. I ask him if he would ever run one of the races, and he tells me he enjoys running. His knees, though, keep him from doing too much of it. But when a German tourist wanted to race from the summit to the lagoon below, Mendoza happily said yes.

“Replacing skiing at Chacaltaya in the future is possible,” he says.

Looking across the dry slope where he learned to ski, the rusted remains of his rope tow, the faded chalet and the memories contained, Mendoza takes a deep breath. At the end of the day, as we drive the winding dirt road down to the city with Chacaltaya shrinking into the distance behind us, he looks ahead.

“It makes me happy when people visit the mountain,” he notes.

Tech Report: Audrie Pelosi’s Couch Was “Always Open to Crash On”

💡 Key Takeaways

  • “She was an exceptional climbing guide and human being,” Apex Adventure Alliance wrote in a statement to Outside.
  • In a recent development, originally from Duluth, Minnesota, Pelosi had long structured her life around her various passions: snowboarding, cycling, and, eventually, an all-encompassing love of climbing and the community around it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Courtesy of Michael Hall).

Audrie Pelosi found climbing after moving to Baraboo, Wisconsin. It wasn’t long before the quartzite cliffs of Devil’s Lake became a cornerstone of her life. She climbed there, worked there, and eventually became its steward as a guide with Apex Adventure Alliance (AAA), bringing fresh climbers to the same arena in which she’d begun.

“She was an exceptional climbing guide and human being,” Apex Adventure Alliance wrote in a statement to Outside. “She was a force in our community and at our guide service. We all will miss her dearly.”.

In a recent development, originally from Duluth, Minnesota, Pelosi had long structured her life around her various passions: snowboarding, cycling, and, eventually, an all-encompassing love of climbing and the community around it. Her passion radiated outwards: she volunteered locally and, in 2026, ran for a Wisconsin Climbers Association board seat, hoping to become more involved in stewardship and community building. “I believe in showing up, doing the work, and listening to the community,” Pelosi wrote in her candidate statement.

“With her friends and community, Audrie was so generous,” noted Garrett Hopkins, AAA’s owner. “That generosity flowed into her climbing, biking, and snowboarding too. When I was living on the road, I knew her couch was always open for a spot to crash if my van was being repaired. She spent countless hours with young climbers in an effort to elevate the safety of the next generation coming up.”.

Industry observers note that pelosi met her husband, Jimmy “The Fox” Robinson, at a snowboard event at Welch Village, Minnesota, and in 2023 the two married atop Mount Bohemia (1,465ft) on Lake Superior. From then on, Pelosi had the nickname “Mrs. The Fox.” One of her friends, Anastasia Exterovich, set up a GoFundMe to raise money for Pelosi’s family in the wake of her passing. She called the pair the “raddest couple.”.

“In my last conversation with Audrie, she joked about selling her handmade bike chain link earrings to anyone who wanted them for ‘free.99,’” Exterovich wrote. “It was such a simple statement made in passing, but it perfectly encapsulated who she was as a person. Even when she didn’t have much, she would give things away freely without hesitation, whether that was earrings, a smile, a laugh, a quick bike tune-up, or a belay.”.

Pelosi passed on May 30, 2026 working as a guide at  Devil’s Lake State Park, teaching a climbing course near the park’s East Bluff. During the course, Pelosi fell from the bluff and suffered fatal injuries. She is survived by her husband, her family, and the broader climbing community in Wisconsin.

#33299. Mandatory Race Gear You’ll Actually Want to Use

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2301 w)

Mandatory Race Gear You’ll Actually Want to Use

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2301 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission.
  • Industry observers note that many ultramarathons, including Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc (UTMB) require runners to carry certain gear.
  • According to recent reports, mandatory trail running race equipment is a lot like American health insurance: We all hate it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

Industry observers note that many ultramarathons, including Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc (UTMB) require runners to carry certain gear. Cade Michael spent years as an unsponsored elite trail runner honing in his mandatory race kit with items that he both genuinely enjoys using and can be found affordably. He did this by taking advantage of sales, buying second-hand, and borrowing from friends. Here he shares his tips for building out your own race kit, including his favorite items in his pack.

According to recent reports, mandatory trail running race equipment is a lot like American health insurance: We all hate it. We’re all tempted to skimp on it. And we all inevitably need it when we’re least prepared. Required gear (or most of it, anyway) doesn’t have to be a waste of money or space. After spending yeas as an unsponsored runner curating my mandatory race gear, here’s my guide to getting gear that you’ll actually want to use more than once every 365 days, including my favorite items in my pack.

UTMB, among other races, often has extensive gear requirements and—whether you like to admit it or not—it’s usually for good reason. Weather and conditions can change rapidly in the mountains, and when you’re pushing your body to the extreme for hours (if not days) on end, as a general rule of thumb, it’s better to have it and not need it than to need it and not have it—particularly for race organizers’ liability insurance.

For example, while it may feel ridiculous for a 100K on the notoriously hot Western States 100 course in Auburn, California to make you carry a rain jacket and emergency blanket, the 2025 Canyons 100K  (on the same trails) saw snow at the start and highs around 40 degrees Fahrenheit. Packing three layers, two pairs of pants, and multiple pairs of gloves might seem like overkill for a day spent backcountry skiing in February, much less a running race in late August, but at the 2025 UTMB, ultrarunning’s most iconic race turned into a game of surviving the winter storm-like conditions.

It has been revealed that I know all too well the allure of going light. But much like Admiral Ackbar’s epiphany at the Battle of Endor, it’s (usually) a trap. At the 2026 Twisted Fork Trail Festival in Park City, Utah, weather forecasts changed drastically in the 48 hours leading into race day, projecting relentless freezing rain. I chucked on a pair of gloves and arm sleeves and figured I’d warm up plenty as the race went on. As soon as we hit the first descent I lost feeling in my hands, feet, legs, cheeks, and plenty of other places I won’t call by name. My heart rate plummeted and I struggled for the entire remainder of the day. Eventual women’s champion, Rachel Drake, on the other hand, donned a warm base layer, long tights, gloves, and vest loaded with extras. Drake is an MD/PhD, mom, and professional runner for Nike ACG. Be more like Rachel, and less like me.

But you don’t have to hate the gear you’re going to buy one way or another to participate in these events.

Sources indicate that quality, packable gear can not only serve to save your race should conditions take a turn through the night in the Alps, but it can also save your run or, heaven forbid, life, if you’re spending any time out on the trails. While you could probably get away with using children’s XXS sized Walmart rain pants, your niece’s tiny pinky swim goggles, and Amazon’s finest two dollar headlamp, you can also use the mandatory equipment list of your next ultra as an excuse to get quality gear that won’t sit at the bottom of your junk drawer until next summer.

Here are my tips and tricks for getting good, lasting gear that’s a little easier on your bank account than the race entry fees and international travel.

Required kit, in most cases, isn’t going to be the product you wear holes through everyday. One is built to be versatile, lightweight, and packable while the other is made for a specific purpose and durability. Some pieces of equipment, like your rain coat for UTMB, are ones you want to stand up in the most brutal of conditions. Others, like a secondary headlamp, are areas you might be able to save some weight and cash.

Lightweight, packable gear is usually updated every year just like the rest of a brand’s product line and often goes on sale during off-season months or discount days (ahem, Black Friday or REI member days). A lot of years, the only update is the colorway, so just get the highlighter yellow and own it!

Industry observers note that better yet, buy gear second hand. Many of the products I’ll list below I grabbed from resale sites like Poshmark or Mercari for a fraction of the retail price.

It may seem obvious, but always get your size. It might seem worth it to save a few grams and get a women’s XXS when you’re in the Chamonix Arc’teryx store panic-buying a rain jacket 24 hours before the gun goes off, but I promise you it’s not. Get the extra ounce and future you will be proud of the responsible decision to get something you’ll actually put on your body.

If you’re questioning whether a piece of gear will satisfy the requirements set by race organizers for your next ultra, err on the side of caution. Get the marginal gains wherever you can within reason, but I promise you trimming two centimeters off your bandaging or emergency blanket will not make Col du Grand Ferret any easier or quicker.

People in your run club and or training partners have probably raced an ultra and used this stuff before. If it’s not something you will need time and time again, it’s OK to borrow it; chances are, they won’t need it in the next week or two anyway. The more you share, the more you save.

According to recent reports, get familiar with your equipment. Try it in training, just like you would a pair of shoes or a nutrition product. Being able to mindlessly locate and use your gear will pay dividends when you have no mindfulness left late into an ultra. Brand-spanking-new isn’t always best.

If you’re between two rain jackets, just get the one with the extra zipper. The best gear is the gear you use. Ruth Croft and Tom Evans won a historically cold and wet UTMB in 2026. When they bundled up through the night, I’m certain they were rocking the clothes they trusted to get the job done, not the ones that came in a few grams under. You’re racing an ultra marathon through the mountains, not a 5K parkrun.

Please keep reading, my opinions are important. Seriously though, whether it’s one of our gear roundups (shameless plug) or your favorite YouTuber, people put dozens of pieces through countless miles so you don’t have to. Take a few extra minutes to read a few pros and cons before you pull the trigger.

It has been revealed that A lot of thought and stress can go into mandatory equipment, but don’t let it take away from the race experience. At my first UTMB race, UTMB Whistler in Canada, the cold-weather gear policy was implemented two days before the race due to a snowstorm. I’d just come from racing in California and Spain in September, so I didn’t have a suitcase stocked with skimpy mandatory equipment. Luckily for me, I couldn’t afford to grab a bunch of last-second gear and just used what I had with me. Retrospectively, my pack was a little heavier and bulkier than it could have been had I been properly prepared, but I didn’t think about the weight once during the race. But boy, was I glad to have warm gloves and a beanie that fit.

Here’s a list of some of my favorite mandatory equipment I’ve amassed over a couple of years of racing in Chamonix as an unsponsored athlete.

Sources indicate that this one is totally optional and, frankly, probably only applicable for a shorter ultra like MCC or OCC during UTMB week. The mini phone is a great tool to have if you’re only out for a handful of hours. So long as you ensure you get a SIM card that has roaming and data enabled for whatever country or region you will be running through, it can call, text, Whatsapp, and even Strava. UTMB requires you to have a smart phone capable of downloading and using the LiveTrail app, and this Google Play Store enabled pocket rocket is the smallest you can get while satisfying the requirements. It also takes pretty cool retro camcorder-style videos. For the longer races like CCC and UTMB, however, it’s probably your safest bet to just bring along your standard, daily driver smart phone. You have to keep your phone on at all times throughout the race, and the number of charging bricks you’d have to haul to keep this thing running through the night outsizes any weight savings it might provide.

Typically, flasks are flasks. Your running vest will usually come with a couple that fit. That being remarked, I usually hate running vests. One of the primary reasons is the way traditional flasks sit in the sleeves, bouncing around and uncomfortably rubbing against my collarbone. My pro tip here is to check out flasks with smaller lids like these Hydrapak pocket flasks. Theoretically, they’re made to fit flush with your running belt, but I’ve found they are less bulky and front heavy in a running vest, too. (As long as they fit in the sleeves.).

A sure bet to be on the required kit list for almost any ultra is a waterproof rain jacket. UTMB’s specifications are rather persnickety, with required minimum waterproof rating, breathability score, sealed seams, and an integrated hood. The On Ultra Jacket lives up to demands while remaining paper thin, uber light, and incredibly packable. It can end up feeling a little too trash-baggy and unbreathable to be your workhorse running jacket, but nevertheless it’s a great piece to be able to throw in your pack anytime you head up into the unpredictable weather of the alpine.

Sources indicate that for headlamps, I always keep a couple of options hanging around for the varying amount of daylight in different races. For OCC, for example, I opt for the Petzl E+Lite. It’s so small and light it’s an almost imperceptible item to carry and it uses nickel-sized 2432 batteries, but, as you might expect, that means it is useless for anything more than an hour or so in a pinch.

Sources indicate that for longer races where you will inevitably be running through hours of darkness, if not the entire night, this is not somewhere to skimp on weight. A popular option in this category is the Petzl Iko Core, which features an incredible 500 lumen bulb, outstanding shine time, and a replaceable battery that sits at the back of the crown for stability. If you’re running UTMB, don’t forget to pick up the mandatory red light filter for fragile wildlife areas.

The crown jewel of mandatory equipment is the running vest. It’s what will hold all of your other mandatory equipment. It’s what will be in direct contact with your body and can make or break the convenience and comfortability of your racing experience. But, most importantly, it’s what will show up in all your post-race photos and make you look either super nerdy or really cool—by which I mean slightly less nerdy. In all seriousness, choosing your hydration vest is critical—and critically personal. Salomon and Nathan offer popular options that have dominated the category dating back to the cradle of civilization. (Hammurabi allegedly kept his chisel in an ADVskin 5L.) But the market is flooding with alternatives as the sport continues to grow, so there is no shortage of options. The most key things to consider are fit and layout. For my preferences, which is for my vest to feel as least like a vest as possible, the Tantrums Crest 6 and Kiprun Pro Team 5L have been excellent. The pocket layouts have tons of nooks and crannies that scratch my obnoxious need for hyperorganization better than keeping foods from touching on my Thanksgiving plate. They have minimal bounce, soft fabric across the shoulder straps, and offer a rear tunnel pocket for an extra flask. Both the Tantrums and Kiprun also come in light colors, a touch that seems a blatant choice for any piece of athletic equipment but was, until recently, a white whale on the hydration vest market.

According to recent reports, A good cap is indispensable and obviously extends beyond race day. It’s not that deep, just get one that feels and looks good. Ciele is a sure fire way to fit in at the coolest run club in town.

In a recent development, waterproof pants can be a tricky one. They’re probably the thing you’ll use the least in everyday training (save for the tinfoil-esque emergency blanket), and they’re one of the most expensive pieces of kit on the list. Getting a pair that satisfies UTMB’s specifications and doesn’t necessitate a 25-liter pack to fit is going to be steep. On makes the Ultra Pant compliment to the aforementioned jacket, but I use these Rab Phantom Pants. The two are kind of “six-one, half-dozen another,” so just grab whichever you can find on a last-season sale.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

(Photo: L to R: Anthony Walsh, Etsy Glass Carabiner Shop, Metolius, Yosemite Climbing Association, Kong).

If you’ve already taken a lap through our gift guide and still need more ideas, we’ve got you. All three of us editors here at Climbing have selected our top picks for gifts this year, from gear we’ve got our eyes on, to accessories in the climbing zeitgeist right now.

Some of these editor gifts picks make perfect mini gifts for stocking stuffers or for that climber partner who you want to thank for giving you the perfect soft catch this past year. Other picks make a bigger impact, from a super lightweight harness to a great gym bag. Most of our picks are great for a variety of climbers, whether it’s your new boyfriend who you hope to convert into a climber, or your mentor who’s been at it for eons.

We hope these gift ideas make your holiday shopping as painless as a splitter hand crack so you can spend more time training or climbing, and less time scrolling through endless product pages and catalogs.

It has been revealed that originally designed and hand-sewn by Nate Barton—the Missoula-based climber who ran the meme account @beta.sprayer until 2024—the Lolo Hoodie V1 ($169.99) is a functional midlayer for cold-weather climbing and the flagship product of the fledgling brand Lolo Hardware. Its large, zippered chest pocket was originally intended to help ice climbers warm up their hands between pitches.

Industry observers note that having pretty much lived in this hoodie for the past three winters, I’ve found the chest pocket far superior to any sort of pant pocket for storing my phone, gloves, and snacks. Plus, with my items against my chest, I never have to worry about my phone freezing or my car keys accidentally slipping out during a chimney. From Joshua Tree in January to Canyonlands in November, this is a comfy and durable hoodie for the coldest days and nights of climbing.

It’s 2026, folks: If you’re still using mined chalk instead of seawater-sourced chalk, this is your call to finally make the switch. Climbing’s feature on the hidden environmental impact of chalk highlighted how the vast majority of magnesium carbonate comes from mines in China, where magnesite factories poison the water and soil of nearby residents.

It has been revealed that luckily, there are plenty of sustainable brands that produce seawater-sourced chalk by using solar power to evaporate ocean brine from seawater. Here are some of our favorites:.

Shop Midnight Lightning Sea Grip Liquid Chalk.

Industry observers note that for climbers with pierced ears, a pair of carabiner earrings is a customizable accessory that never gets old. Recently, I’ve been getting tons of compliments on my pair of silver, locker draw earrings (yes, they actually screw and unscrew!) that I bought at the Yosemite Climbing Museum in July. You can buy them here, but stock is limited. In case they sell out, here are a few other great places to buy carabiner earrings online:.

Recent findings suggest that after breaking a cross-loaded carabiner in a scary trad fall, I now always add some sort of tape or rubber band to keep cam carabiners in place. I wrote about my DIY solution a couple of years ago, but now I simply slide on Avant Climbing’s Flip-Stop Cam Carabiner Stabilizers ($22.50 for a 10-pack). The Flip-Stop makes for easy cam clipping when mega pumped. But unlike my rubber band hack, it also keeps the cam sling open for clipping a long draw into. Crucially, like a quickdraw’s dogbone, the Flip-Stop prevents carabiners from rotating onto the dangerously weak X-axis. Nothing ruins the holidays like a pair of broken ankles.

The latest Arc’teryx Alpha SL Harness ($180) may weigh less than the gift wrap paper you’ll hide it in. At an absurdly light 78 grams (2.7oz), the Alpha SL is for those going ultralight in the mountains, whether that’s an alpine rock romp or a substantial ski traverse. This harness is also surprisingly comfortable to rappel in, thanks to its uber-stiff Aluula-composite construction. And it fits a range of body types thanks to its adjustable leg loops and five waistbelt sizes. Just don’t set it down unattended on a glacier—it’ll blow away in the slightest gust of wind.

Shop Arc’teryx Alpha SL Harness.

In a recent development, the Patagonia Airshed Pro Pullover ($169) might have been built for mountain running, but I wear mine year-round on all sorts of objectives, from sunny rock climbs to cold north faces. The Airshed Pro is a pseudo-windlayer: decently breathable for high-output activities, yet stills blocks the wind and has a water-repellent coating. The result is a shirt equally at home skiing on a glacier or rambling up a gusty rock ridge.

A note on sizing: Since the Airshed Pro was originally designed for runners, the cut is quite slim. I size up to facilitate a wider range of motion.

It has been revealed that I have been loving the Black Diamond Solution Hoody ($299) as a light fall belay jacket and even for cold rock climbing when I’m too chilly to shed my jacket. The Solution manages to be super lightweight, movement-friendly, and breathable, yet warm. This is largely because the specific PrimaLoft insulation used in this jacket is made with technology developed by NASA for astronauts. Here on earth, it also works great. It honestly does feel like being wrapped in warm air.

According to recent reports, the pocket real estate is also generous, and it’s nice that the whole thing packs into the left hand pocket so you can easily stash it in your pack without a cam or crampon tearing into the insulation. I’m also looking forward to using this as a mid-layer below a shell for ice climbing this winter.

Unless you’ve been living under a rock (which many of our readers hopefully have), you’ve heard about the upcoming film about the weed plane that crashed into a Yosemite lake in 1976. What followed was a tragicomic climber gold rush. Now, to mark the 50th anniversary of the incident, you can sport one of several new t-shirts or hats ($29.95-$44.95) memorializing this infamous moment in Yosemite climbing history. All proceeds support the Yosemite Climbing Association and the Yosemite Climbing Museum.

In a recent development, have I used one? No. Do I desperately want one? Yes. As a 5’2” climber, I’m often just a few inches short of being able to make the clip from a good stance. I’ve heard wonderful things about the stiffy Kong Panic Draw ($54.95-$59.95) that lets you clip bolts otherwise out of reach. Maybe 2027 will be the year I finally gift myself one! If there’s a short or easily panicked sport climber in your life, I bet they would be stoked to get this as a present. Or you could make one for them DIY-style yourself.

Recent findings suggest that the oversized, durable Metolius Climbers Tote ($64.95) has become my go-to gym bag. It easily fits my personal gear plus a 60m rope, or four sets of personal gear (shoes, harness, and chalkbag for me, my husband, and my two kids). Despite having stored weathered climbing shoes zippered inside for too long, this bag miraculously doesn’t stink yet either. It stows away nicely in gym cubbies (whereas my previous Cotopaxi tote would sort of spill out) and is easy to carry by hand or shoulder. This is a great mid-sized gift for the climber in your life, or you could fill it with other gear you’re gifting for a bigger impact.

Industry observers note that note on price: While this tote isn’t on sale at REI, co-op members get 20% off one full-price item through Nov. 30, so this is a good one to save on.

I receive a lot of climbing books and galleys to review and consider for coverage. Only some of them are so good that I can’t put them down. That’s how I felt about Erratica, a new collection of true stories from Moab-based, life-long climber Brian Laidlaw. Rare is the read that both keeps you attentive and entertained, yet also evokes deeper reflection. With Erratica, Brian manages to do just that. Pick up a copy ($20) at Moab’s Back of Beyond bookstore, or find one online anywhere books are sold.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kayaking is among the outdoor recreation activities available in Grand Theft Auto VI’s Mount Kalaga National Park, where players can paddle along wooded waterways.

Recent findings suggest that many gamers have waited 13 years for a newly introduced Grand Theft Auto (GTA)  game so they can steal cars, rob banks, and wreak havoc in a fictional American city. I had a slightly different mission. I wanted to go hiking.

GTA VI, the long-awaited installment in Rockstar Games’ blockbuster franchise, arrived November 19 with an enormous open world set in Leonida, a fictional state modeled after Florida. Beyond the game’s cities and beaches are mangrove swamps, forested mountains, and a surprising number of opportunities for outdoor recreation.

Industry observers note that among them is an entire national park that some fans believe was inspired by Georgia’s Providence Canyon State Park. Naturally, as a journalist who covers the outdoors, I decided to investigate.

Getting there was its own expedition. I spent several hundred dollars on a PlayStation 5 specifically for this assignment, endured a download that initially threatened to take 14 hours, and worked through introductory missions involving a robbery and a dubious boating operation before I could drive north to the game’s national park—Mount Kalaga.

Located near Leonida’s northern border, Mount Kalaga is one of six major regions players can explore, with a vast stretch of mountainous backcountry offering hunting, fishing, and off-road trails, according to Rockstar’s official description. It took me about 20 minutes of real-life driving to get there from the game’s starting point, though my tendency to crash into medians at full speed probably added a few minutes to the trip.

Recent findings suggest that mount Kalaga isn’t especially faithful to real-world park rules. Hunting is generally prohibited in U.S. national parks unless specifically authorized, while off-road vehicle use is restricted. Still, the park’s layout, scenery, and recreation options reflect an impressive effort to make the fictional outdoors feel like somewhere worth visiting.

The drive into the park looks a lot like Northern California, with winding roads cutting through steep, lush hillsides. Farther in, the landscape opens up to waterfalls, rocky cliffs, and wide waterways bordered by dense vegetation, with forested islands and bridges stretching across the valleys below.

Recent findings suggest that more impressive than the landscape was how well the game designers captured the everyday details of an actual national park. They included designated trailheads, road markers, and even went so far as to build public restrooms that look unpleasantly familiar to anyone who’s ever used the real deal. The park also has a visitor center with a wooden porch, green railings, tourists milling around outside, and a sign above the entrance reading, “True wanderers are never lost.”.

Sources indicate that it holds far more wildlife than I managed to spot in one visit, too. Rockstar told gaming publication Game Informer that Leonida contains more than 170 animal species, and The Guardian reported that players can identify 62 types of birds using binoculars and record them in a wildlife logbook.

Inside Mount Kalaga National Park, I found designated hiking trails dotted with wildflowers and packed with both sporty dog walkers and out-of-breath tourists alike, alongside an elaborate, technical mountain bike trail system. Complete with marked access routes, wooden bridges, and built-out ramps and drops, it looked like a legitimate, and genuinely difficult, trail network, with a time-trial mode built in for players looking to race the course.

I acquired my mountain bike in a way that probably wouldn’t go over well at an actual trailhead; I stole it from a group of unsuspecting riders taking in the view of the lower valley.

After exploring on foot and two wheels and evading a gaggle of angry policemen looking for a bike thief, I paddled a red kayak through a wooded waterway and took a park-service-looking off-road vehicle onto the dirt roads.

Next, I decided to hot-wire a vacant ATV from a trailhead parking lot and set off on a backcountry joyride. From an overlook, I watched rivers wind between tree-lined islands as the sun set, and later, at the top of Mount Kalaga, I looked up at a sky full of stars as the sound of crickets drifted out of the game and into my living room.

What began with a frantic search for the last PlayStation 5 in stock at Target and a virtual armed robbery, ended with a peaceful evening in what might be the most meticulously detailed national park ever created for a video game.

Colorado Trail and Continental Divide Trail ‘Extensively Damaged’ After Severe Flooding: Here’s What We Know

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (863 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This article was updated on November 18, 2026, at 11:48 a.m.
  • In just over a week, two massive flooding events hit southwestern Colorado, destroying homes, businesses, and infrastructure across numerous mountain towns.
  • In a recent development, “Rebuilding these damaged sections will not be quick, easy, or cheap,” Paul Talley, executive director of the Colorado Trail Foundation (CTF), said in a November 5 upgrade on the floods.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This article was updated on November 18, 2026, at 11:48 a.m. with additional information regarding the condition of the Colorado Trail section 28 and the Continental Divide Trail.

In just over a week, two massive flooding events hit southwestern Colorado, destroying homes, businesses, and infrastructure across numerous mountain towns. But property is not all that the floods affected. Parts of both the Continental Divide Trail (CDT) and the Colorado Trail (CT) suffered damage that locals and trail organizations are calling “extensive” and “severe”, and which could take a very long time to repair.

In a recent development, “Rebuilding these damaged sections will not be quick, easy, or cheap,” Paul Talley, executive director of the Colorado Trail Foundation (CTF), said in a November 5 upgrade on the floods. “But we are committed to rebuilding.”.

As many of these areas are still inaccessible, there is very little confirmed information on their current state. Videos circulating online show missing bridges at key river crossings, and reports from the USFS and other agencies indicate that trailheads are damaged, and “heavy debris” is blocking some sections. But there has yet to be a full, official report on damage to these trails.

Here is what we know so far based on official updates, local reports, and videos.

Junction Creek is the CT’s southernmost section. Its trailhead, just outside of Durango, is also the CT’s southern terminus. Junction Creek Trail crosses multiple footbridges over the creek along its 19-mile stretch. A video posted to Instagram reveals the Junction Creek trailhead sign that many hikers use for their CT terminus photo now standing directly at the edge of a tall wash filled with flood debris.

“Junction Creek Trail #553 suffered a near-total loss in places where it parallels and crosses Junction Creek,” a USFS conditions report from November 13 reads. “Miles of trail as well as multiple bridges crossing Junction Creek were wiped out, replaced with massive piles of boulders, trees, and other flood debris.”.

According to recent reports, according to the report, both the lowest trail bridge at 2.6 miles from the trailhead and the Walls Gulch Trail Bridge at 14.6 miles were destroyed. One social media video reveals the first footbridge washed away completely. The USFS posted its own video of the road to Junction Creek to Facebook, showing a “20-foot waterfall” over the edge of the destroyed road.

“There is no doubt that trails across the forest have suffered severe damage,” the San Juan National Forest wrote.

Sources indicate that in an interview with The Gazette, Talley mentioned, “The Colorado Trail Foundation has never experienced an event that damaged this much trail. This is the largest section of trail ever damaged in our 52 years.”.

Industry observers note that authorities claim that recovery work will likely begin in spring and carry into summer 2027 due to weather. They discouraged hikers from even attempting to set out on the area’s trails.

Sources indicate that “Record flooding across Southwest Colorado has left San Juan National Forest roads, trails, and other infrastructure inaccessible, severely damaged, and, in many cases, impassable,” a USDA Forest Service Facebook post reads. “Don’t become a statistic—rescue will not be readily available due to the current demand for search and rescue services.”.

The CTF said that it will be working over the winter with USFS, local partners, and volunteers to determine timelines and project budgets for the restoration efforts.

“It will be months before we can better understand what the next steps need to be on the sections damaged by climate events this season,” wrote Talley in his November 5 update.

There is even less information regarding damage to the CDT, which also passes through the flood-affected areas of Southwestern Colorado.

The Continental Divide Trail Coalition (CDTC) posted on Facebook on October 23, warning hikers that flooding had made “travel to and from the CDT trailhead at Wolf Creek Pass impossible,” and that “hikers may need to make alternate plans to avoid the area.”.

On November 2, the CDTC posted another update for CDT travelers. “The extent of damage to the CDT, access roads, and CDT communities is still unknown,” it said. While the interactive map on its website shows no current closures of the trail due to flooding, the CDTC advised hikers to use “extreme caution and check with local authorities before visiting.”.

According to recent reports, outside of Colorado, Fresh Mexico also experienced severe flooding. However, Audra Labert with the CDTC told Backpacker, “The area of New Mexico near the southern terminus did not experience significant damage from flooding.”.

While the full extent of the damage to these trails remains to be seen, what’s certain is that the CTF, CDTC, USFS, and other state agencies have a great deal of restoration work to do next summer. Volunteers will be in high demand, and Talley, of the CTF, promised to be open about how hikers can help.

“While we do not yet know what it will take to rebuild, we do know what we will need,” Talley wrote. “We will need our supporters, we will need our dedicated volunteers, and we will need that community spirit that makes the CT so special.”.

#33295. Breaking: Stephanie Case Just Ran 100 Miles in Antarctica. She Doesn’t Even Like the Cold.

Breaking: Stephanie Case Just Ran 100 Miles in Antarctica. She Doesn’t Even Like the Cold.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1541 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 2025, a photo of Stephanie Case breastfeeding her infant daughter, Pepper, at an aid station during a 100K ultra in Northern Wales went viral, and the human rights lawyer and ultrarunner became the face of postpartum badassery.
  • According to recent reports, now, she’s officially the first woman to run 100 miles in Antarctica.
  • “The whole idea for this race came after I had my daughter and people were asking me if I was going to start to settle down,” Case, 44, shared with Trail Runner from her home in Chamonix, France.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 2025, a photo of Stephanie Case breastfeeding her infant daughter, Pepper, at an aid station during a 100K ultra in Northern Wales went viral, and the human rights lawyer and ultrarunner became the face of postpartum badassery.

According to recent reports, now, she’s officially the first woman to run 100 miles in Antarctica. Case took on the November 8 challenge in part to prove that the things she did before becoming a mom weren’t behind her. If anything, she could come back and do them even better.

“The whole idea for this race came after I had my daughter and people were asking me if I was going to start to settle down,” Case, 44, shared with Trail Runner from her home in Chamonix, France. “They were criticizing me after I came back for my first race postpartum, telling me that I was selfish to be taking that time to train. So I wanted to go out and really prove to myself and remind myself that I could keep doing big things.”.

Actually, big is an understatement. Of the eight runners who started the Antarctic Ice Ultra 100 miler on Union Glacier, Case was one of four finishers, and second overall. Her finishing time of 17 hours, 31 minutes and 39 seconds, a clip of 10:31 per mile, smashed the former overall course record by five hours. Only Yusheng Ni, a top ultrarunner from China with experience racing in Antarctica, ran faster in a latest best-ever mark of 17:02:24.

Here’s the kicker: Case doesn’t even like running in the cold.

There’s cold, and then there’s Antarctica cold. The race started at 1 a.m. under a 24-hour sun, with temperatures as low as minus 35 degrees Fahrenheit—roughly 35 degrees colder than a typical kitchen freezer. And with fierce polar winds, no exposed skin is safe.

According to recent reports, “I’m someone who doesn’t like when the house goes below room temperature. My partner and I are constantly having a fight about where we set the thermostat,” Case shared. “So this was going to be a big challenge for me. I knew that I wasn’t going to love it. But I’m Canadian. There’s no bad weather, there’s just bad clothing, they say.”.

In a recent development, finding the right gear was one of the biggest priorities in Case’s preparation. She reached out to other runners who had completed the Antarctic 100-miler in previous years to glean their insight. One offered an unexpected tip: Apply sunscreen inside of her nostrils, since the sun reflecting off the snow can burn there, too.

She also worked with The North Face, one of her sponsors, to design a custom shoe specifically for the conditions. Breathability was key: She didn’t want moisture trapped inside the shoe, and the sole needed to remain flexible in extreme temperatures. There was also the matter of laces. Frozen laces—or having to tie them with mittens on—were not an option. The solution was a BOA closure system, which let her tighten the shoes by turning a dial. The design also included an integrated, insulated but breathable gaiter and removable spikes she could screw into the soles if conditions got icy.

The setup worked better than she could have hoped. Case wore two pairs of socks—a thin liner underneath a wool pair—and didn’t change them once during the entire race.

Recent findings suggest that “I just set it and left it,” she remarked. “And it was one of the things I was most stressed about, because with hands, you can put on more gloves. You can have hand warmers. But toe warmers don’t work when you’re running. They can’t fit in the shoe. And I knew if my toes were cold, I was just going to be screwed. And they were toasty the whole time.”.

As for the rest of her clothing, Case had to consider another challenge: her sweat rate.

“I’m a heavy sweater. Even in just mild cold temperatures, I sweat a liter an hour, and in warm temperatures up to two liters,” she stated. “So I knew that I would be at a pretty big disadvantage, because when you sweat, your gear gets wet and then you’re screwed.”.

According to recent reports, her strategy was to dress as lightly as possible through her core while keeping her hands, feet and face warm and protected. In the coldest stretches, she wore winter tights under wind pants, along with a thin base layer, a midlayer, and a shell on top. At some points, she stripped down to a thin base layer and shell.

“As long as I kept moving, I was fine,” she said. “But I wouldn’t be able to kind of stop and walk if something went wrong.”.

Industry observers note that she never quite felt warm, and some exposed skin on her face did get frostbitten. But she managed to find moments of equilibrium.

It has been revealed that “I felt comfortable at times. And then other times I feel like I was just constantly on the edge,” she remarked. “I wasn’t freezing, but I was cold. But as long as my feet were OK and my hands were OK, then I was fine to keep moving.”.

Recent findings suggest that the temperature wasn’t the only feature of Antarctica that concerned Case. She describes herself as a “mountain goat.” Living in Chamonix, she’s accustomed to steep trails and vert—not the flat, repetitive terrain of Antarctica’s 38-loop course.

Working with her coach, Meghan Roche, she shifted her training toward flatter ground and faster running. The change paid off: during her workouts, Case set personal records at several distances, from the 10K through the marathon.

“I had a love-hate relationship with it,” she said of the training. “But the funny thing was that every time I had a training session, I was getting PRs, because I just don’t run on flat ground.”.

According to recent reports, she also tested her gear in a cryotherapy chamber during a trip to Geneva, Switzerland, spending 20 minutes in temperatures that gradually warmed from minus 148°F to minus 22°F. The goal wasn’t so much to acclimate as to understand what the cold would feel like and test her logistics. The session made her rethink her fueling plan: Pulling off gloves, unzipping a shell, and drinking from a flask in those conditions would be too cumbersome.

Recent findings suggest that instead, her camera operator doubled as her crew, handing her a SIS gel and flask every loop. While most competitors visited the aid tent every lap or two, Case aimed to go ten loops—roughly a marathon—between stops. She had to cut the first stretch short when her balaclava froze into a solid block of ice, but after that she managed three 10-loop stints.

The aid station offered some reprieve, with ramen noodles, mashed potatoes, shots of maple syrup, and Rice Krispies treats, but even small tasks there got complicated. Taking her gloves off for just 30 seconds to go to the bathroom could mean waiting 20 minutes for her hands to warm up again.

“There was not a single minute during this race when I kind of just relaxed and allowed myself to switch off,” she states. “In any other 100, I can usually just kind of push past [discomfort], but there, one tiny mistake could end the race for me.”.

It has been revealed that as Case recovers at home with collagen mask treatments to heal her frostbitten cheeks and nose, her next challenge is already on the calendar: becoming the first woman to complete the Montane Arctic Spine, a 500-kilometer race in February. This time, she’ll be on Nordic skis, pulling a sled and traveling solo, with checkpoints as far as 50 miles apart. She’ll need to melt her own snow, pitch her own tent, and carry out the journey without a crew.

She hopes Antarctica has prepared her for an even harder task.

“Sometimes the way to get through a really scary thing is to line up an even scarier thing afterwards,” she remarked.

Beyond that, Case is developing a project called “94 Degrees,” a film that will show her running the gamut of conditions from minus 40 degrees Celsius in the Arctic to 54 degrees Celsius at Badwater in California’s Death Valley, a 94-degree Celsius spread. (She’s qualified for Badwater but still needs to apply for an invitation, so that part isn’t yet confirmed.).

Sources indicate that and in the meantime, she’ll continue her work for the U.N. while serving as the President of Free to Run, a non-profit organization that uses sport to empower women and girls in conflict-affected areas. And she’ll soak up all the cuddles she can with Pepper, now 2, while sharing stories of that one time she ran 100 miles in Antarctica. It’s a story that almost sounds like a fairy tale.

According to recent reports, “I actually brought one of her toys, a penguin rubber ducky, with me on the trip, just as a reminder of her,” Case noted. “And then this penguin came out on the course and actually ran alongside me for part of it. I’ve been showing her photos and videos … but still … it’s all kind of unbelievable.”.

Breaking: A Climber We Lost: Jun Kyu Kim

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (914 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that on August 21, 2026, Jun Kyu Kim was scrambling on the approach to a climb in Eldorado Canyon, when he fell.
  • Born on April 3, 1981, Jun was raised by his loving parents Hyoun Sook Kim and Ho Young Kim, and grew up in Chicago with his two sisters.
  • Sources indicate that jun once remarked that climbing was the thing he lived for.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Courtesy Gisely Ferraz).

Industry observers note that on August 21, 2026, Jun Kyu Kim was scrambling on the approach to a climb in Eldorado Canyon, when he fell. Even though he was wearing a helmet, he suffered a fatal head injury. The tragedy shook the Denver climbing community he had been a part of. Jun touched so many lives, whether through Cruxing in Color, of which he was an early supporter, or at the crag, where he was known to offer kind advice and encouraging words. He leaves behind his loving family, his girlfriend, and so many friends whose lives were made better by his generosity and kindness.

Born on April 3, 1981, Jun was raised by his loving parents Hyoun Sook Kim and Ho Young Kim, and grew up in Chicago with his two sisters. Throughout his life, Jun was known for his adventurous spirit and zest for exploration. He discovered his love for the outdoors—where he found peace and joy—at an early age during a National Outdoor Leadership School trip to Alaska. It was during high school that he was introduced to rock climbing, which quickly became his true passion.

Sources indicate that jun once remarked that climbing was the thing he lived for. In the climbing community, he was known for his trademark red hat, dirtbag clothes, love for donuts, and his patented naps. He could sleep anytime and anywhere, then upon waking, send his project. After completing a route, he’d often be out like a light. Ever a favorite climbing partner, he exuded confidence, patience, and calm under pressure. And he settled people’s nerves, allowing them to achieve ever harder things. When friends would get down on themselves about their climbing, he was always the first to remind them to not take climbing so seriously, to have fun, and to give themselves grace on high gravity days.

I spoke with Jun’s girlfriend, Sz-min Harley, and his best friend, Shawnee, to learn more about what Jun meant to the people he climbed with. Many people saw him as a mentor. He would frequently take less experienced climbers under his wing. But he also was famous for sandbagging. If you accepted his suggestion, you knew you could be in for a far more difficult adventure than you had counted on. But Jun’s encouraging words, infectious laughter, and love for fun would make it all worth the story in the end. Shawnee says that the first time they climbed together was in El Salto, where he had Shawnee try his warm-up. She could barely get halfway up before she had to come down. Jun refused to tell Shawnee the grade, but she later found out it was a 5.12b.

Jun was also known for his love of cooking, something that he learned from his mom at a young age. He continued to cook with her until the end. For Jun, food was a love language. He liked few things better than bringing people together around a meal, whether in the kitchen or around a campfire. The first time he came to visit Shawnee, he drove six hours and showed up with a cooler full of homemade Korean dishes for her to try. Once, he cooked dinner for the 20 people who had signed up for his friends’ newly launched Beyond Jamming crack climbing clinic in Indian Creek. The entire crew came back from a full day of climbing, tired and hungry, to a grinning Jun. He had made homemade tacos for everyone, complete with vegetarian, gluten-free, and lactose-free options.

That was Jun—a man with an unbelievably massive heart who was always looking for a way to help and who showed up every day for his friends. He was the kind of friend who would always be there for you, whether you needed a belay on a project or a partner willing to head out to that route tucked away in a far corner of the desert. Never letting the friendship fade, Jun was known for checking in on the people he loved, making sure you knew that he was thinking of you. He would help fix your van, make you chicken soup when you were sick, and send you a card just to say he was glad you existed. Not only did Jun give love from the bottom of his heart, but he did it without expecting anything in return.

Jun’s friend Adien shared something that has stuck with me: “Jun was a rare, selfless climber. He would go to the crag for himself, but he would go for you.”.

Recent findings suggest that climbing took Jun all over the world—Thailand, Greece, Columbia, Cuba, Chile, Mexico. But until the end, his favorite place was always Indian Creek. The first time he went, he and a friend only had four cams that they bumped up the routes, bearing miserably cold weather. Yet, the Creek still managed to claim his heart. Over the years, that love became even stronger and more special. Season after season, he made memories of hard sends, campfires, and laughter with his friends. For those who loved him, the Creek will never be the same.

Forty five years around the sun would never be enough, but Jun managed to fill those years with more life than most people do in twice as much time.

We miss you, Jun, and we will always carry you with us, keeping your spirit alive by choosing generosity, connection, and care.

Tech Report: Grand Theft Auto 6 Is Here. Goodbye, Winter Training Plan.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (750 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On my run this morning, the streets of New York seemed a little emptier.
  • Across the country, a lot of people have come down with a sudden and very specific illness.
  • Here’s the thing, though: for a game about crime, a surprising amount of it is about nature.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On my run this morning, the streets of New York seemed a little emptier. You may have noticed the same thing in your part of the world. It is not the Rapture. It’s Grand Theft Auto.

Across the country, a lot of people have come down with a sudden and very specific illness. Even the man who profits from it saw this coming. Back in April, Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick noted, “I think a lot of people will be calling in sick on November 19.” One economist puts the cost in lost productivity at around $1 billion. To be fair, it’s been a long wait. GTA V came out 13 years ago. My daughter was in daycare then. (That was the only time I could sneak in some game time.) She is now a freshman in high school.

Here’s the thing, though: for a game about crime, a surprising amount of it is about nature. I mean, there’s a National Park you can explore. It’s been less than 24 hours, and my Instagram feed has already served up players feeding NPCs (the game’s random bystanders) to alligators and a Bigfoot lurking near a swamp called Cottonmouth Lake. The Bigfoot is the Skunk Ape of actual Florida folklore. It knocks you out with noxious fumes, and the last thing you see is a pair of giant hairy feet coming toward you. In its demented way, it’s a Florida nature documentary. Which is to say: you are about to lose a lot of people to the swamp.

In a recent development, then there’s the time commitment. Rockstar Games says one of its studio heads needed about 80 hours to get through the story, side quests included. That’s a 16-week marathon build at five hours a week. For those of us with a training plan to execute, a ski trip on the calendar, and a whole winter we’d actually like to spend outside, the math is cruel. Like me, you may be suffering from GTA FOMO.

When GTA IV came out in 2008, it was easily the best game I’d ever played. It was set in Liberty City, a barely disguised New York City. Niko Bellic, the main character of the game, had a story that was darker and more grown-up than anything the series had tried before: a war-haunted immigrant chasing the American dream through its back alleys, with the pathos of a Michael Mann criminal. Plus it was fun to just walk the streets. That spring I interviewed Dan Houser, one of the game’s creators, for GQ. I asked him why New York was the perfect setting. “You just meet freaks everywhere,” he told me. He described a guy who walks up with a CD player and asks if you like hip-hop, “the real stuff.” Say yes, and it turns into a little scene with people laughing at you. “We were inspired by living here.”.

This newly introduced GTA received the same obsessive treatment, this time in Florida. Rockstar has had a research team based in Miami for years, and its developers have described riding along with ex-cops, hitting the clubs, and logging beach time, all so that Leonida, the game’s version of Florida, would feel like a real place.

I never finished GTA V. Its release coincided with new fatherhood and a new gig, and, well, I chose to be a responsible adult. I’m told this was the right call. My character is presumably still sitting in a stolen car somewhere outside SoCal inspired Los Santos, engine running, waiting for me. To be honest, I didn’t love it the way I loved IV anyway. But VI, if all the reviews are correct, is a masterpiece. My kids now know how to operate the microwave. So I will be playing it.

In a recent development, meanwhile, the real outdoors isn’t going anywhere, and neither is my list: I’ll be hiking in Mexico next week, off-roading in Texas in December, and maybe squeezing in a ski trip. But there is GTA that must be played. I believe in you. You can do both. Run in the morning, steal cars at night. Don’t neglect your children or your pets if you have them. But if you miss a few runs, fine. Maybe that spring race isn’t the one where you go for the PR, you know?

So take some comfort: as you hunker down this winter, you are still communing with nature, technically. Just watch out for the alligators.

The 9 Best Snowshoes of 2027

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2842 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

  • In a recent development, if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission.

  • It has been revealed that after a season of snowshoe-testing in blizzards, sub-zero temps, and alpine ice, our top pick is the MSR Revo Explore ($290) for its light weight, flexibility, and impressive grip.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
